body:
Literature beyond poetry and religion

Ancient Indian literary traditions included systematic works on grammar, political administration, medicine, mathematics, astronomy and other branches of knowledge. These works frequently took the form of Shastras, Sutras and Samhitas.

A Shastra is a systematic treatise on a particular subject. A Sutra commonly presents knowledge through concise rules or aphorisms. A Samhita is an organised collection of material, although its precise meaning varies according to the subject.

Major scholarly works

AuthorWorkSubject
PaniniAshtadhyayiSanskrit grammar
PatanjaliMahabhashyaGrammatical commentary
AmarasimhaAmarakoshaSanskrit lexicon
KautilyaArthashastraStatecraft, administration and economy
Bharata MuniNatyashastraDrama and performing arts
VatsyayanaKamasutraHuman relationships and social life
CharakaCharaka SamhitaMedicine
SushrutaSushruta SamhitaMedicine and surgery
AryabhataAryabhatiyaMathematics and astronomy

Panini's Ashtadhyayi systematised Sanskrit grammar through a structured collection of rules arranged into 8 chapters. Patanjali's Mahabhashya is an important grammatical commentary associated with the Paninian tradition. It should be distinguished from the Yoga Sutras, traditionally associated with a figure also named Patanjali.

The Arthashastra is traditionally attributed to Kautilya, also identified with Chanakya. It discusses the duties of rulers, taxation, administration, trade, diplomacy and state security. The surviving text contains material developed over time, so its entire contents should not automatically be treated as a description of the Mauryan administration.

Fables, stories and narrative collections

Narrative collections communicated practical wisdom, morality and social experience through entertaining stories.

WorkTraditional authorLiterary character
PanchatantraVishnu Sharma5-part collection of instructive stories and fables
HitopadeshaNarayanaDidactic collection influenced by earlier narrative traditions
DashakumaracharitaDandinProse narratives concerning 10 princes
KathasaritsagaraSomadevaExtensive Sanskrit collection of stories

The Panchatantra frequently uses animals as characters to convey practical lessons about friendship, judgement, conduct and political wisdom. It travelled beyond India through translations and adaptations.

Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, composed in 11th-century Kashmir, preserves narrative material associated with the earlier Brihatkatha tradition. It demonstrates how ancient stories were reworked in medieval Sanskrit literature.

Biographies and historical narratives

Banabhatta, associated with the court of Harshavardhana in the 7th century CE, composed the Harshacharita, a literary biography of Harsha. He is also associated with Kadambari, a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance.

Kalhana composed the Rajatarangini in 12th-century Kashmir. Although it belongs chronologically to the medieval period, its use of Sanskrit continues the classical historical and literary tradition. It presents a chronological account of Kashmir's rulers and uses earlier records and traditions.

Royal inscriptions and literary patronage

Literary expression was also used in royal inscriptions. A Prashasti praises the qualities, achievements, ancestry or victories of a ruler. Because it was commonly produced under royal patronage, it combines historical information with deliberate praise.

The Prayaga Prashasti, composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, celebrates the achievements of the Gupta ruler Samudragupta. It is inscribed on the pillar at Prayagraj that also bears earlier Ashokan inscriptions.

The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman

The Junagadh rock inscription of the Western Kshatrapa ruler Rudradaman I, dated approximately 150 CE, is an important example of early extensive Sanskrit inscriptional prose.

It records the repair of the Sudarshana Lake near Girnar in Gujarat. The inscription also recalls earlier construction and improvements associated with the Mauryan period.

The record is important for both political history and literary history. It demonstrates the use of elaborate Sanskrit for royal public communication at a time when earlier inscriptions had frequently employed Prakrit.

Prakrit and Sanskrit inscriptions

Most Ashokan edicts were composed in Prakrit. Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription is in Sanskrit. The spread of Sanskrit in inscriptions was gradual and did not immediately eliminate Prakrit or regional languages.

Prelims focus

  • Panini wrote Ashtadhyayi; Patanjali is associated with Mahabhashya.
  • Kautilya's Arthashastra concerns statecraft and administration.
  • Banabhatta is associated with Harshacharita and Kadambari.
  • Kalhana's Rajatarangini concerns the history of Kashmir.
  • Harishena composed the Prayaga Prashasti of Samudragupta.
  • Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription is an early extensive Sanskrit inscription associated with Sudarshana Lake.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapters 7 and 12, pp. 65–74 and 127–134; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 29–40; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 4, pp. 30–33; Central Sanskrit University, About Sanskrit, sections on grammar, Shastra and narrative literature, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Three royal inscriptions trace growing Sanskrit use from predominantly Prakrit Ashokan edicts, without implying complete language replacement.
pictures.caption: Important stages in ancient inscriptional literature

title: Ancient Scholarly Literature, Narrative Collections and Royal Inscriptions

body:
What is vernacular literature?

Vernacular literature refers to compositions produced in languages commonly used by particular regional or linguistic communities. In medieval India, languages such as Gujarati, Marathi, Bengali, Kannada, Telugu, Assamese, Punjabi, Awadhi and Braj developed extensive literary traditions.

The medieval growth of vernacular literature did not mean that Sanskrit disappeared. Sanskrit continued to be used in scholarship, religion and poetry, while Persian became important in administration and courtly culture under several medieval states.

Medieval India was therefore characterised by the coexistence of classical, courtly and regional languages.

The development of regional languages

Many North Indian regional languages belong to the Indo-Aryan language family. Their historical development involved earlier Indo-Aryan forms, including Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrits and later Apabhramsha varieties.

Apabhramsha refers to several late Middle Indo-Aryan linguistic forms used extensively in literary compositions. Jain authors contributed significantly to Apabhramsha literature, particularly in western India.

Gujarati, Marathi, Bengali and several other Indo-Aryan languages emerged through gradual regional linguistic changes. They did not arise simultaneously from a single uniform form of Apabhramsha.

Southern languages such as Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to the Dravidian language family. They have their own linguistic histories, although their vocabularies and literary traditions were influenced by Sanskrit.

Language-family distinction

Gujarati, Marathi and Bengali belong to the Indo-Aryan group. Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to the Dravidian family. Sanskrit influence on a Dravidian language does not make that language Indo-Aryan.

Why regional literature expanded

Religious communication

Bhakti saints and Sufi teachers communicated spiritual ideas through familiar languages. Their compositions could be understood by audiences who had no formal training in Sanskrit, Arabic or Persian.

Political and courtly patronage

Regional kingdoms supported local poets, scholars and literary institutions. Rulers commissioned translations, heroic narratives and chronicles to celebrate political achievements and establish cultural authority.

Growth of towns and social groups

Artisans, merchants, cultivators, religious communities and urban groups participated in new forms of devotional and literary expression. Oral recitation, pilgrimage and public gatherings helped compositions circulate beyond royal courts.

Important examples of regional literary development

Language or regionLiterary development
MalayalamUse in inscriptions under the Cheras of Mahodayapuram; later literary interaction with Sanskrit
KannadaEarly courtly literature followed by important Jain and Virashaiva compositions
TeluguEpic adaptations, religious poetry and royal patronage
BengaliEpic adaptations, Mangalakavya, Vaishnava biographies and oral traditions
MarathiDevotional compositions of the Varkari tradition
GujaratiJain literary compositions, Bhakti poetry, narrative literature and bardic traditions

The development of Malayalam illustrates the relationship between regional identity and literary patronage. The Cheras of Mahodayapuram used Malayalam in inscriptions from approximately the 9th century. Malayalam also interacted extensively with Sanskrit in literature.

The 14th-century work Lilatilakam discusses the grammar and literary conventions of Manipravalam, a mixed literary idiom combining Sanskrit and Malayalam. The term literally means ruby and coral.

Persian, Hindavi and Urdu

Persian became an important language of courtly and administrative communication under the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire. Its interaction with Indian languages influenced vocabulary and literary expression.

Hindavi was used as a broad historical designation for certain regional forms of speech in northern India. Poets such as Amir Khusrau employed Persian and Hindavi in their literary activities.

Urdu developed through the historical interaction of northern Indian Indo-Aryan speech forms with Persian, Arabic and other linguistic influences. Its development was gradual and involved cultural centres in northern India as well as the Deccan.

Dakhini emerged as an important literary form associated with the Deccan. It demonstrates that the development of Urdu literary traditions was not confined to Delhi.

The regional adaptation of classical narratives

The spread of the Ramayana and Mahabharata into regional languages illustrates how vernacular literature could combine inherited narratives with local cultural expression.

Regional workAuthorLanguage
Ramavataram, commonly called Kamba RamayanamKambanTamil
Krittivasi RamayanaKrittivasa OjhaBengali
RamcharitmanasTulsidasAwadhi
Saptakanda RamayanaMadhava KandaliAssamese

These works contributed to regional literary identity and made classical narratives accessible to new audiences through familiar vocabulary, local expressions and devotional themes.

Prelims focus

  • Apabhramsha contributed to the development of several Indo-Aryan regional languages.
  • Jain authors played an important role in western Indian literary traditions.
  • Lilatilakam is associated with Manipravalam and Malayalam literature.
  • Kamban composed a Tamil Ramayana; Krittivasa composed a Bengali Ramayana.
  • Persian was important in medieval courtly and administrative culture.
  • Trap: Urdu was not created at a single moment by a single poet, and medieval regional literature did not replace Sanskrit completely.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 9, pp. 122–137; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 9, pp. 226–231; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, p. 41; IGNOU, A History of Gujarati Poetry, Unit 6, Section 6.2, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Indo-Aryan development and the independent Dravidian family, with Sanskrit influence across both and Persian contact with northern literary traditions.
pictures.caption: Language families and medieval literary development

title: The Formation of Medieval Regional Languages and Literary Cultures

body:
Devotion as a literary tradition

Bhakti refers to personal devotion to the divine. Bhakti literature expressed love, surrender, remembrance, ethical conduct and the relationship between the individual and God through hymns, poems and narrative compositions.

Its growth helped establish regional languages as important literary mediums. Many devotional compositions circulated orally before being collected into organised anthologies.

The Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu

From approximately the 6th century CE onwards, important devotional movements emerged in southern India. Their poet-saints travelled between sacred places, composed hymns in Tamil and expressed intense devotion to particular deities.

TraditionAlvarsNayanars
Devotional orientationVaishnavismShaivism
Traditionally recognised number1263
Important figuresAndal, Nammalvar, PeriyalvarAppar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Karaikkal Ammaiyar
Major literary collectionNalayira Divya PrabandhamTevaram and other Tamil Shaiva collections

The Nalayira Divya Prabandham is a collection of approximately 4000 sacred Tamil compositions associated with the Alvars. Its religious importance led to its recognition within the tradition as the Tamil Veda.

The Tevaram contains hymns associated with Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. Another major Tamil Shaiva devotional work is the Tiruvacakam, associated with Manikkavasagar.

Andal was a woman Alvar whose compositions express devotion to Vishnu. Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman poet associated with the Shaiva devotional tradition. Their literary participation demonstrates that women were important contributors to early Bhakti movements.

Temple patronage

The Chola and Pandya rulers supported several Tamil devotional institutions. Between approximately the 10th and 12th centuries, royal patronage helped preserve and organise devotional poetry, connect sacred places with major temples and maintain the recitation of hymns.

Bhakti literature was therefore shaped both by the contributions of individual saints and by institutions capable of preserving their compositions.

The Virashaiva tradition of Karnataka

During the 12th century, Basavanna and other religious teachers developed the Virashaiva or Lingayat movement in Karnataka. Important figures included Allama Prabhu and Akkamahadevi.

Their principal literary form was the Vachana, a concise Kannada devotional utterance expressed through direct and accessible language.

Virashaiva literature emphasised personal devotion to Shiva and questioned ritual exclusiveness, caste restrictions and established social inequalities. The direct language of the Vachanas enabled complex religious and ethical ideas to reach a wider audience.

The Varkari tradition of Maharashtra

The Varkari tradition centres on devotion to Vithoba, also called Vitthala, at Pandharpur in Maharashtra. Vithoba is regarded as a form of Vishnu or Krishna.

Marathi devotional literature in this tradition developed through several saints.

SaintWork or literary formPrincipal contribution
JnaneshwarJnaneshwariMarathi explanation of the Bhagavad Gita
NamdevDevotional poetry and AbhangsPersonal devotion to Vithoba
EknathEknathi BhagavataCommunication of devotional teachings in Marathi
TukaramAbhangsDevotion, ethical conduct and criticism of hypocrisy
ChokhamelaDevotional poetryExpression of devotion despite caste exclusion

The Jnaneshwari, also called Bhavarthadipika, was composed in the 13th century. It made the philosophical and devotional teachings of the Bhagavad Gita accessible through Marathi.

An Abhang is a Marathi devotional poetic composition closely associated with the Varkari tradition. Namdev's literary influence extended beyond Maharashtra, and some compositions attributed to him are included in Sikh scripture.

Prelims focus

  • The 12 Alvars were Vishnu devotees; the 63 Nayanars were Shiva devotees.
  • Nalayira Divya Prabandham belongs to the Alvar tradition.
  • Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar are associated with Tevaram.
  • Basavanna and Akkamahadevi are associated with Kannada Vachana literature.
  • Jnaneshwari is a Marathi explanation of the Bhagavad Gita.
  • Trap: Vachana belongs principally to the Kannada Virashaiva tradition; Abhang to the Marathi Varkari tradition.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 104–111; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, pp. 142–150; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints, pp. 36–40, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

title: Bhakti Literature of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Maharashtra
